_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: For his Paschal offering and for his guilt offering: we have not found a female guilt offering or a female Paschal offering.
rashi:a3.1: This is the reading: “For nothing renders a substitute except what grazes until it becomes blemished.” That is, nothing renders a substitute except that which is consecrated with inherent sanctity, so that if it is not fit to be sacrificed it is not sold without a blemish but is left to graze. Therefore Rabbi Shimon holds that with a guilt offering and a Paschal offering, since their name does not take effect on a female, it is sold without a blemish, and so it does not render a substitute. But with a burnt offering, where there is burnt offering status for a bird, he holds that it grazes and renders a substitute.
rashi:a4.1: Since a leftover Paschal offering is sacrificed as a peace offering: therefore, since peace offerings belong to the Paschal offering, and peace offerings come from females; and even though this female is not sacrificed even as a peace offering after Passover, as we said above (Temurah 19a) that if it remained after Passover it grazes, nevertheless the status of a peace offering is upon it, since it is female [and a peace offering may be female], and inherent sanctity descends upon it.
rashi:a5.1: Since a leftover guilt offering is sacrificed as a burnt offering: and it turns out that this female of the guilt offering is a burnt offering, so it should be consecrated with inherent sanctity as a female burnt offering, for we have found a female burnt offering among birds.
rashi:a5.2: For communal gift offerings: and even if it is a burnt offering, since it stands to become a communal burnt offering, it does not render a substitute.
rashi:a7.1: For his bull: the bull of Yom Kippur, which is a sin offering; for there is sin offering status upon it, since we find the red heifer, which is called a sin offering (Ḥullin 11a).
rashi:a7.2: It is consecrated for Temple maintenance: it is not sacrificed on the altar, and that is why he calls it Temple maintenance; that is, it has the law of Temple maintenance.
rashi:a9.1: These are two bodies: an individual and a king [nasi]. In the body of an individual you do not find a male goat as a sin offering, and in the body of a king you do not find a female goat. But a female burnt offering you do find in this same body: if he wishes he can renounce ownership of his property and become poor, and a bird burnt offering is fit for him.
rashi:a10.1: He sinned before he was appointed: [the questioner reasons that] there is sin offering status upon it in this same body, since if he sinned now he would be obligated to bring a male goat.
rashi:a11.1: He does not bring a bird burnt offering [Rashi’s heading adds, in parentheses, “he is wealthy”]: if he were obligated to bring a burnt offering he would not bring a bird burnt offering, since he is wealthy. And even if he is poor, a voluntary burnt offering is not brought in the form of poverty unless he explicitly specified a bird.
rashi:a12.1: Rabbi Shimon holds in accordance with Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya: that even for an unspecified gift offering of a wealthy man, a bird burnt offering is fit.
rashi:a14.1: And their monetary value is allocated with the rest of the property for Temple maintenance: for Rabbi Eliezer holds that unspecified consecrations are for Temple maintenance, even an animal; yet something fit for the altar never leaves the altar’s claim. And Rabbi Yehoshua holds that a person does not forgo the sanctity of the altar and consecrate for Temple maintenance something that is fit for the altar; therefore, presumably he consecrated them for the altar, and they themselves are sacrificed as burnt offerings.
rashi:a15.1: And the females are sold etc., and he brings burnt offerings with their money: for when he did not specify, he consecrated them as a burnt offering.
rashi:a16.1: Their status stems from deferred sanctity: since the males are sacrificed as burnt offerings and the money of the peace offerings goes for burnt offerings, it follows that he holds that, unspecified, he consecrated them as a burnt offering. It is then a case of one who designates a female for a burnt offering, so how can it be sacrificed as a peace offering? It needs to graze, as our mishna teaches (above, Temurah 18b): One who designates a female for a burnt offering, it grazes.
tosafot:a3.1: For nothing renders a substitute except what grazes and becomes blemished: that is, that which is consecrated with inherent sanctity, so that if it is not fit to be sacrificed it is not sold without a blemish but grazes. Therefore Rabbi Shimon holds that with a guilt offering and a Paschal offering, since a guilt offering and a Paschal offering do not take effect on a female, it is sold without a blemish, and therefore they do not render a substitute. But with a burnt offering, where there is burnt offering status for a bird, he holds that it grazes and renders a substitute. [This is] Rashi’s wording.
tosafot:a5.1: Rabbi holds in accordance with the Rabbis, who say that leftovers go to communal gift offerings, and there is no substitute for a communal offering: This is puzzling: what is he saying? Above it implies that he makes substitution depend on grazing, and here it implies that he makes grazing depend on substitution. Let him say that they graze and render a substitute! It seems that this is the explanation: since they go to communal gift offerings, and there is no substitute for a communal offering, one cannot say that it helps one who designates a female for a guilt offering to be consecrated with inherent sanctity because a leftover guilt offering is sacrificed as a burnt offering. For their law is not the same: a guilt offering renders a substitute, and a leftover guilt offering does not, since it goes to communal gift offerings, which do not render a substitute. It is not like one who designates a female for a Paschal offering, for a leftover Paschal offering becomes a peace offering, which renders a substitute just as the Paschal offering itself does. Therefore it is right that inherent sanctity should take effect on a female he designated for a Paschal offering, for it is all the same whether he designated it for a Paschal offering or for a leftover Paschal offering, that is, a peace offering, since both render a substitute.
tosafot:a6.1: Since it has burnt offering status: with regard to a poor man, in the bird burnt offering. As it now enters your mind, [the case] means one who designates a female for his burnt offering, for example a wealthy leper who must bring a male animal as a burnt offering. That is why it says that he renders a substitute when he designated a female for his burnt offering: because this very obligation he owes applies to a female if he were poor, for he would designate a bird burnt offering, which may be female, since unblemished status and maleness do not apply to birds. That is why it took the case of a poor man, such as a poor leper: in this very obligation that he owes there is a female burnt offering.
tosafot:a7.1: Since there is the heifer of purification [parat ḥatat]: This is puzzling according to what I explained, that a female burnt offering can be found within the very obligation he owes, whereas here one cannot say so. Furthermore, why did it take the heifer of purification? Most sin offerings of the altar come as females! One can say that he objects a fortiori: even one who designates a female for a burnt offering, which itself is not fit for a burnt offering, [Rabbi Shimon] nevertheless says renders a substitute because it has burnt offering status from the bird burnt offering. All the more so one who designates a cow for his bull, since the cow itself is fit to be a heifer of purification if it is red, so we should say that it is consecrated.
tosafot:a8.1: An individual who designated a male goat for his female goat, it should be consecrated, since there is the king’s goat: He could equally have objected from the baraita itself above, about a guilt offering that must be one year old and he brought one two years old, where Rabbi Shimon says that they are not consecrated at all. But why not? It is fit for the guilt offering for misuse of consecrated property and for robbery! And the answer given here applies to it as well.
tosafot:a9.1: These are two bodies: Rashi explained: an individual and a king; in the body of an individual you do not find a male goat as a sin offering, and in the body of a king you do not find a female goat, but a female burnt offering you do find in this same body, since if he wishes he can renounce his property and become poor, and a bird burnt offering is fit for him. End of his words. But this does not seem right to me, for what does it object shortly after, “If so, here too he does not bring a bird burnt offering”? Either way the cases are not alike, since he himself is fit for a female burnt offering if he renounces his property. Therefore it seems to me to explain “these are two bodies” thus: this individual is not fit to become king while the king is alive, and the king is not fit to have the status of an individual; but poor and rich are like one body, for the rich man is fit to become poor and the poor man fit to become rich. Now the objection is sound: if so, as he said, “He did not sin [as king] and was not obligated to bring a male goat,” even though his body was fit to become king, since at the time he sinned he was not obligated to bring a male goat, it is not called one body; so too here, at the time he sinned he was not obligated to bring a bird burnt offering, and he cannot discharge his obligation with it.
tosafot:a12.1: Rabbi Shimon holds in accordance with Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya etc.: he brings a turtledove or pigeons. That is, since he can discharge his obligation with a bird even after designating an animal, as is stated in chapter Merubba (Bava Kamma 78b), it rejects [the objection] well with regard to a female burnt offering. And one must say that Rabbi Shimon’s case of one who designates a female for his burnt offering is now dealing with one who says, “It is incumbent upon me to bring a burnt offering,” who can discharge his obligation with a female bird burnt offering even after designating an animal, as is stated in chapter Merubba (also there).
tosafot:a14.1: They are sold for the needs of burnt offerings, and their monetary value is allocated with the rest of the property for Temple maintenance: for Rabbi Eliezer holds that unspecified consecration is for Temple maintenance, and it is like one who consecrates unblemished animals for Temple maintenance, which never leave the altar’s claim.
tosafot:a15.1: And Rabbi Yehoshua says the males themselves are sacrificed as burnt offerings: for he holds that a person does not forgo sacrifices of the altar and consecrate for Temple maintenance something that is fit for sacrifices of the altar, and his unspecified intention is for a burnt offering, which is burned entirely to the Name.
gershom:a1.1: For his Paschal offering and for his guilt offering, which are his obligation, it does not render a substitute, since it is consecrated only for its value. For nothing renders a substitute except something that grazes and becomes blemished: what has so much sanctity in it that it requires grazing renders a substitute. But one who designates a female for a guilt offering, since [Rabbi Shimon] holds that it is sold without a blemish, and likewise one who designates a female for his Paschal offering, therefore they do not render a substitute.
gershom:a2.1: [Rabbi said: I do not agree with the statement of Rabbi Shimon with regard to the Paschal offering. Rather, it certainly renders a substitute, since a leftover Paschal offering is sacrificed as a peace offering; a female too has the law of a leftover Paschal offering, and with its money a peace offering is sacrificed; it is consecrated with inherent sanctity and renders a substitute, for peace offerings come from females.] And let him also teach: I do not agree with the statement of Rabbi Shimon with regard to a guilt offering; rather, it renders a substitute, since we said above in the mishna that a leftover guilt offering is sacrificed as a burnt offering. This female too is like a leftover guilt offering and should be sacrificed as a burnt offering, for we find a female burnt offering in the bird burnt offering; so it should be consecrated with inherent sanctity and render a substitute.
gershom:a3.1: Rabbi holds: [that] the leftovers, which are sacrificed as burnt offerings, [go to communal gift offerings].
gershom:a4.1: They go to communal gift offerings: to communal burnt offerings, and there is no substitute for a communal offering.
gershom:a5.1: Who designated a female cow for his bull: his own bull, which he brings on Yom Kippur as his sin offering.
gershom:a6.1: It should be consecrated and render a substitute: for we have found the heifer of purification, the red heifer, which is female and is called a sin offering.
gershom:a7.1: In any case this is no proof, for the heifer of purification is consecrated for Temple maintenance, and such items have no substitute, since they are not consecrated with inherent sanctity; so there is no difficulty from it.
gershom:a8.1: An individual, who brings a ewe or a female goat as his sin offering, and designated a male goat for his female goat: it should be consecrated with inherent sanctity and render a substitute, since sin offering status is upon it, for a king brings a male goat as his sin offering. [The answer:] It is not like the case here, and that is why it is not consecrated: an individual and a king are two bodies, and what this one brings, that one does not bring. But here, with an individual who designates a female for his burnt offering, it is consecrated, for he himself, if he is poor, or if he wishes to renounce his property and become poor, can bring a female bird burnt offering.
gershom:a9.1: They sinned before they were appointed as king: if he designated a male goat for the female goat that he is obligated to bring, since he was still a commoner, it should be consecrated, for if he sinned now, after he was appointed, he would need to bring a male goat; here the commoner and the king are one body.
gershom:a10.1: Even so, it is not alike. There, the reason he does not bring a male goat, even though he is one body, is that he did not sin when he was king and was not obligated to bring a male goat; therefore if he brings a male goat [for a sin committed] when he was a commoner, it is not consecrated.
gershom:a11.1: If so, here too: with one who designates a female for his burnt offering, it should not be consecrated, for one who designates an animal [for a burnt offering] is wealthy and cannot bring a female bird burnt offering. [Rather, this is Rabbi Shimon’s reason with regard to a burnt offering: he holds that a wealthy man too can bring a bird burnt offering, in accordance with Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya.]
gershom:a12.1: Rabbi Yehoshua says: The males themselves are sacrificed as burnt offerings, [and the females are sold for the needs of peace offerings and he brings burnt offerings with their money. His reason is explained in the last chapter, Yesh BeKodshei Mizbe’aḥ: a person does not forgo sacrifices of the altar, something fit for the altar to be wholly for the fires, and consecrate them for Temple maintenance. Furthermore, he holds that a person divides his vow: the animals for sacrifices of the altar and the rest of the property for Temple maintenance.
gershom:a13.1: How can the females be sacrificed as peace offerings? From his saying that the males themselves are sacrificed as burnt offerings,] it follows that he consecrated all the animals as burnt offerings, and a female cannot be sacrificed as a burnt offering; so how can it be sacrificed as a peace offering? These peace offerings come from deferred sanctity, since he consecrated them all as burnt offerings and it is not fit for a burnt offering.
gershom:a14.1: Another version: Is this to say [that he consecrated them with] inherent sanctity? He consecrated all of them as a burnt offering, for the fires.
gershom:a15.1: But they require grazing: the females, since they come from deferred sanctity.
gershom:a16.1: Rabbi Yehoshua holds in accordance with Rabbi Shimon, who said “it is sold without a blemish”: anything that is not itself fit for sacrifice, inherent sanctity for that offering does not descend upon it. Therefore it does not require grazing, but is sacrificed as a peace offering.
gershom:a17.1: Say that Rabbi Shimon said: that inherent sanctity does not descend upon it, with regard to a female for a guilt offering.
gershom:b1.1: Where there is no guilt offering status: upon it, for a female. But with a female for a burnt offering, where there is burnt offering status for a female, even Rabbi Shimon concedes that it is consecrated with inherent sanctity.
gershom:b2.1: In addition, we have heard: that he said that for his burnt offering it renders a substitute; evidently it is consecrated with inherent sanctity, so how can they be sacrificed as peace offerings? Rabbi Yehoshua holds in accordance with the other tanna’s view of Rabbi Shimon etc., who said that even for his burnt offering it does not render a substitute.
gershom:b3.1: The substitute of a guilt offering: even a male; their offspring: when the substitute is female.
gershom:b4.1: Or the offspring of their offspring, they graze: for we hold that whatever is left to die in the case of a sin offering is left to graze in the case of a guilt offering, and the substitute of a sin offering is left to die.
gershom:b5.1: And their money is allocated for communal gift offerings: since the money of a leftover guilt offering is sacrificed as a burnt offering.
gershom:b6.1: Rabbi Eliezer says: They are left to die: as the Gemara explains, that he decreed after atonement on account of before atonement.
gershom:b7.1: Rabbi Elazar says: He brings a burnt offering with their money, as an individual’s gift offering.
gershom:b8.1: A guilt offering whose owner died, or whose owner achieved atonement: with another guilt offering, and the first remained: it grazes etc.
gershom:b9.1: And it is necessary: for them to disagree explicitly in both, in the substitute of a guilt offering and in a guilt offering whose owner died.
gershom:b10.1: As, had it taught us: only one, a guilt offering whose owner died or achieved atonement, in this Rabbi Eliezer says they die because he decreed after atonement on account of before atonement. For if you say that after they achieved atonement it grazes, there is a decree lest people say [the same] before they achieved atonement, when both are standing, [one for atonement and one for grazing], and he would set one aside for grazing before he achieved atonement with the other. That is not proper: since he is obligated to bring his guilt offering and both are fit for a guilt offering, he should not leave one to graze until he has achieved atonement with its fellow. That is why he says it dies.
gershom:b11.1: But with regard to the substitute of a guilt offering and the offspring of the substitute: here there is nothing to decree, since its law is always to graze, whether before atonement or after atonement. One might say that he concedes to the Rabbis that they graze; it is necessary to state that here too [he says] they die, for he decreed these on account of those, a guilt offering whose owners died or achieved atonement.
gershom:b12.1: Another version: had he taught only the substitute of a guilt offering, which is the first clause, I would have said that there the Rabbis disagree because it might be exchanged: for if you say the substitute of a guilt offering dies, there is a decree lest it be exchanged for the guilt offering itself and the guilt offering itself be left to die. Therefore they say [it grazes], for if they are exchanged, when he notices he has a remedy: he can go back, bring it and sacrifice it. But in the latter clause, a guilt offering whose owners died or achieved atonement, there is no exchange, [since there is] only one guilt offering; I would say they do not disagree but [hold] it dies. That is why he taught the latter clause, to show that here too they disagree. And had he taught [only] a guilt offering whose owners died, in this Rabbi Elazar [so the text; the sense seems to require Rabbi Eliezer] says it dies, because it cannot be exchanged, as there is no other; but the substitute of a guilt offering etc.
gershom:b13.1: Not taught: that [the dispute about] the offspring of the substitute of a guilt offering, which according to the Rabbis grazes and according to Rabbi Elazar he brings a burnt offering with its money, [applies] only after atonement, after he achieved atonement with the guilt offering itself and this one remained.
gershom:b14.1: But before atonement: if he has not yet achieved atonement with it, and both are standing, the guilt offering itself and the offspring of its substitute.
gershom:b15.1: Everyone agrees that it itself: the offspring itself, if he wishes [to sacrifice it as a guilt offering, he may sacrifice it], for he can achieve atonement with whichever he wishes, since both are males.
gershom:b16.1: Rava said: There are two refutations of the matter: [One, that a person cannot achieve atonement] with the increment of consecrated property through an item that comes from a transgression, for this offspring comes from a substitute, which came through a transgression, as it is written: “He shall not exchange it.”
gershom:b17.1: And in addition, didn’t Rav Ḥananya teach: at the beginning of our chapter, that the second offspring is not sacrificed? And this offspring of a substitute is a second offspring, for the substitute itself is a first offspring, since it comes by the force of the offering. Rather, if it was stated, it was stated like this.]
gershom:b18.1: Not taught: that the Rabbis and Rabbi Elazar disagree except before atonement, for before atonement he cannot sacrifice it as a guilt offering, as a person cannot achieve atonement through an item that comes from a transgression.
gershom:b19.1: But after atonement, everyone agrees that the offspring itself is sacrificed as a burnt offering, for a burnt offering does not come for atonement. But didn’t Rav Ḥananya teach [in support] that the second offspring is not sacrificed at all? It is difficult.
gershom:b20.1: Another version: “Everyone agrees that the offspring is sacrificed as a guilt offering.” Rava said: Two refutations etc. And in addition, didn’t he teach etc. Rather, say: he brings a burnt offering with its money as an individual’s gift offering, since the second offspring is not sacrificed. Some say: they disagree only before atonement, for the Rabbis hold that this offspring is a leftover guilt offering, which grazes and its money is allocated for gift offerings, and Rabbi Elazar holds [it is] for an individual’s gift offering; but after atonement, since it is male and fit for sacrifice, they hold that it itself is sacrificed as a burnt offering. But didn’t Rav Ḥananya teach etc. Rather, say: he brings a burnt offering with the money of the second offspring, since there is burnt offering status [on it].
gershom:b21.1: And let him resolve it from Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina, who said above: Rabbi Elazar concedes with regard to one who designates a female for a guilt offering.
gershom:b22.1: He never heard it: [Rabbi Avin bar Ḥiyya] never learned it [the text has “Rav Kahana”, corrected in brackets]. “Rabbi Elazar concedes.” “What”: that is, what did Ravin bar Kahana answer him?
gershom:b23.1: Rabbi Elazar says that its offspring is sacrificed as a burnt offering only with regard to one who designates a female for a burnt offering, where there is burnt offering status for a female; but with regard to a guilt offering, where there is no guilt offering status for a female, he concedes that its offspring is not sacrificed as a burnt offering. [Rabbeinu Gershom has Rabbi Elazar himself concede, where the printed text reads “even Rabbi Eliezer concedes”.]
gershom:b24.1: He said to him: The reason of Rabbi Elazar, with one who designates a female for a burnt offering, that its offspring is sacrificed as a burnt offering, is not because there is burnt offering status on its mother but because it is fit for a burnt offering, since it is male; and this one too, the offspring of the guilt offering, is male and fit for a burnt offering.
rashi:b1.1: Where there is no guilt offering status for its mother: for we have not found a female [guilt offering].
rashi:b2.1: Renders a substitute: evidently inherent sanctity descends upon it, so that it must graze. A Jerusalem version reads: How can the females be sacrificed as peace offerings? Their bodies are consecrated as a burnt offering; that is, they need to graze, for we say (Bava Kamma 78b) that if he wishes he can discharge his obligation with a bird burnt offering, that is, with a female burnt offering.
rashi:b2.2: In addition, Rabbi Shimon said: that it is consecrated in its body, for we established above that Rabbi Shimon holds in accordance with Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya.
rashi:b4.1: Mishna: The substitute of a guilt offering, whether male or female, grazes, for it is learned as a halakha [transmitted from Sinai] (above, Temurah 18a): whatever is left to die in the case of a sin offering is left to graze in the case of a guilt offering.
rashi:b4.2: The offspring of a substitute: for example, if he exchanged [another reading: designated] a female for his guilt offering, and it gave birth.
rashi:b5.1: He brings a burnt offering: for the leftovers go to an individual’s gift offering.
rashi:b6.1: But isn’t a gift offering also a burnt offering: this is said as a statement [not a challenge]; rather, it goes on to explain what the difference between them is.
rashi:b6.2: When it comes as an obligation [Rashi’s text reads “as an obligation” where ours reads “as a burnt offering”]: that it is incumbent on the individual to sacrifice it, he places his hands on it etc.
rashi:b6.3: And if he was a priest: the one who designated the guilt offering, achieved atonement with another, and the first was consigned to grazing.
rashi:b6.4: Its service and its hide: of the burnt offering that comes from the leftover.
rashi:b6.5: Are his: he himself sacrifices it and takes the hide, even if he is not of the priestly watch serving that week. For so it is taught: From where is it derived that a priest may come and sacrifice his offerings at any time and at any hour he wishes? The verse states: “And he comes with all the desire of his soul… and he shall minister” (Deuteronomy 18:6–7); in Bava Kamma, at the end of the first chapter HaGozel (Bava Kamma 109b).
rashi:b7.1: And he does not place his hands on it: for a communal offering has no placing of hands, except the bull for an unwitting communal sin and the scapegoat, since we have a tradition of two placings of hands in a community; in Menaḥot, chapter Shetei Middot (Menaḥot 92a).
rashi:b7.2: And although he is a priest: that is, even if he is a priest, its service and its hide belong to the men of the priestly watch, since it is communal, and a priest of another watch may not sacrifice it, as it is written: “Beside that which is sold according to the fathers’ houses” (Deuteronomy 18:8): what did the fathers hand over to one another? I in my week and you in your week.
rashi:b8.1: Gemara: And it is necessary: for Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis to disagree about two cases.
rashi:b9.1: As, had it taught us a guilt offering whose owner achieved atonement: in that case Rabbi Eliezer says it dies, because he decreed after atonement, when he achieved atonement with the first [i.e., with another animal]. If you say he brings a burnt offering with the money of the leftover, people would come to say so before atonement too: if a blemish befell it, they would come to bring a burnt offering with its money, and he would commit a prohibition, for as long as he has not achieved atonement its money stands for a guilt offering.
rashi:b10.1: But the substitute of a guilt offering: where one cannot say this, for even before atonement the substitute of a guilt offering does not stand to be sacrificed, as that is how it is learned [as a tradition].
rashi:b10.2: Say he concedes: Rabbi Eliezer [concedes] that it grazes. Another explanation, a Jerusalem version: had it taught us about a substitute, in that case Rabbi Eliezer says that it and its offspring die because they might be confused. Since both are standing, the consecrated animal and the substitute, one might err and exchange them, leaving the first to graze and taking the substitute for the guilt offering; since in the end its money is sacrificed, he would not care whether he sacrifices it, and he would commit two prohibitions: one, that he sacrifices the substitute, and further, that he brings a burnt offering with the money of the guilt offering when he has not yet achieved atonement, since the substitute does not atone for him, as we say below that an item that comes from a transgression does not atone for a sin, and a substitute comes from a transgression, as he transgressed “He shall not exchange it.” But a guilt offering whose owners achieved atonement will not be confused, for if the first was found before the second achieved atonement we do not care which is sacrificed and which grazes; so one might say that he concedes to the Rabbis etc.
rashi:b12.1: It itself: the offspring of the substitute is sacrificed as a guilt offering, if the first was lost.
rashi:b13.1: Through a transgression: for with a substitute he transgressed “He shall not exchange it” (Leviticus 27:10). And although the substitute of a burnt offering and of a peace offering is sacrificed, those do not come for atonement.
rashi:b13.2: And Rav Ḥananya [taught] in support of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi [Rashi’s heading reads “Rav Ḥanina”]: above in this chapter (Temurah 18b).
rashi:b13.3: The second offspring is not sacrificed: and this is a second offspring, since he calls the substitute an offspring, as it comes by the force of another.
rashi:b14.1: The dispute: about the offspring of a substitute before atonement. There Rabbi Eliezer said it dies, for if you say it grazes, since its money is sacrificed, they would come to confuse it and sacrifice it as a guilt offering; and the Rabbis say that since it itself is not sacrificed as a burnt offering, they would not come to confuse it. But after atonement, where one cannot speak of confusion, the offspring itself is sacrificed as a burnt offering.
rashi:b16.1: From Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, who said: above, “Rabbi Elazar concedes etc.” And we learn from it that the reason of Rabbi Eliezer [so Rashi’s text; the statement above is Rabbi Elazar’s] with regard to the offspring of one who designates a female for a burnt offering is that there is burnt offering status on its mother; but here, where there is no burnt offering status on its mother, it is not so.
rashi:b18.1: Because it is fit to be sacrificed: the offspring.
rashi:b19.1: He raised an objection: it is our mishna, “The substitute of a guilt offering etc.”
rashi:b19.2: He brings a burnt offering with their money: he cited the statement of Rabbi Elazar.
tosafot:b6.1: If he was a priest, its service and its hide are his: that is, if this priest to whom the leftover belongs, he himself sacrifices it and the hide is his, even if he is not of the priestly watch serving that week. For so it is taught: From where is it derived that a priest may come and sacrifice his offerings at any time and at any hour he wishes? The verse states: “And he comes with all the desire of his soul… and he shall minister”; in Bava Kamma, at the end of the first chapter HaGozel (Bava Kamma 109b). [This is] Rashi’s wording.
tosafot:b12.1: But before atonement, everyone agrees that it itself is sacrificed as a guilt offering: And if you say: is this offspring better than its mother? Its mother is not sacrificed as a guilt offering, since it is a halakha transmitted to Moses from Sinai that the substitute of a guilt offering is not sacrificed as a guilt offering. One can say that perhaps he holds that where the substitute of a guilt offering is female, [its offspring] may indeed be sacrificed as a guilt offering before atonement, since the halakha was learned only about a substitute that is itself fit for a guilt offering, such as a male; but after atonement all leftovers go to gift offerings. And afterward, when he says “the dispute is before atonement,” he holds that the substitute too, its money is sacrificed as a burnt offering.
tosafot:b13.1: A person cannot achieve atonement through an item that comes from a transgression: and a substitute comes from a transgression, as he transgressed “He shall not exchange it.” And although the substitute of a burnt offering and of a peace offering is sacrificed, those do not come for atonement. [This is] Rashi’s wording.
tosafot:b13.2: The second offspring is not sacrificed: the offspring of a substitute is like a second offspring. My teacher, the Ramar, asked: what is the objection? Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi spoke according to Rabbi Shimon, and the Rabbis disagree with him, holding that all offspring are sacrificed until the end of the world. And he answered that the objection is to his saying “everyone agrees,” even Rabbi Eliezer. And [Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi] says that even according to the Rabbis the first offspring is sacrificed and the second offspring is not; evidently the second is inferior to the first. If so, according to Rabbi Eliezer, who says in the mishna that the first offspring is not sacrificed, all the more so the second.
tosafot:b17.1: But with regard to a guilt offering, where there is no burnt offering status on its mother: Here one cannot explain that there is no burnt offering status on its mother from the bird burnt offering, since there is burnt offering status on its mother from the bird burnt offering. Rather, this is the explanation: the initial consecration of its mother was not as a burnt offering, for it was consecrated as a guilt offering.
tosafot:b19.1: With their money, yes; themselves, no: My teacher, the Ramar, found this puzzling: what is the objection? The reason that here [the offspring] itself is not sacrificed is that it might be confused, as stated above, and that reason does not apply to one who designates a female for a guilt offering. And he answered that it seems to him that those reasons above were said only about the substitute itself, but the offspring carries the rejection of its mother; so how can you say, with one who designates a female for a guilt offering, that its offspring itself is sacrificed as a burnt offering? And so too we must say above in our chapter, that he objects from this mishna here to Rabbi Elazar, who says: One who designates a female for a burnt offering and it gave birth, it itself is sacrificed as a burnt offering.
